{{Short description|Theorem in measure theory}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2020}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''disintegration theorem''' is a result in [[measure theory]] and [[probability theory]]. It rigorously defines the idea of a non-trivial "restriction" of a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] to a [[measure zero]] subset of the [[measure space]] in question. It is related to the existence of [[conditioning (probability)|conditional probability measures]]. In a sense, "disintegration" is the opposite process to the construction of a [[product measure]].

==Motivation==
Consider the unit square <math>S = [0,1]\times[0,1]</math> in the [[Euclidean plane]] <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>. Consider the [[probability measure]] <math>\mu</math> defined on <math>S</math> by the restriction of two-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]] <math>\lambda^2</math> to <math>S</math>. That is, the probability of an event <math>E\subseteq S</math> is simply the area of <math>E</math>. We assume <math>E</math>  is a measurable subset of <math>S</math>.

Consider a one-dimensional subset of <math>S</math> such as the line segment <math>L_x = \{x\}\times[0, 1]</math>. <math>L_x</math> has <math>\mu</math>-measure zero; every subset of <math>L_x</math> is a <math>\mu</math>-[[null set]]; since the Lebesgue measure space is a [[complete measure|complete measure space]],
<math display=block>E \subseteq L_{x} \implies \mu (E) = 0.</math>

While true, this is somewhat unsatisfying. It would be nice to say that <math>\mu</math> "restricted to" <math>L_x</math> is the one-dimensional Lebesgue measure <math>\lambda^1</math>, rather than the [[trivial measure|zero measure]]. The probability of a "two-dimensional" event <math>E</math> could then be obtained as an [[Lebesgue integration|integral]] of the one-dimensional probabilities of the vertical "slices" <math>E\cap L_x</math>: more formally, if <math>\mu_x</math> denotes one-dimensional Lebesgue measure on <math>L_x</math>, then
<math display=block>\mu (E) = \int_{[0, 1]} \mu_{x} (E \cap L_{x}) \, \mathrm{d} x</math>
for any "nice" <math>E\subseteq S</math>. The disintegration theorem makes this argument rigorous in the context of measures on [[metric space]]s.

==Statement of the theorem==
(Hereafter, <math>\mathcal{P}(X)</math> will denote the collection of [[Borel measure|Borel]] probability measures on a [[topological space]] <math>(X, T)</math>.)
The assumptions of the theorem are as follows: <ref>{{Harvard citation no brackets|Bogachev|2007|loc=§10.4, §10.6}} </ref> 
* Let <math>Y</math> and <math>X</math> be two [[Polish space|Polish spaces]] (i.e. [[separable space|separably]] [[Completely metrizable space|completely metrizable spaces]]).
* Let <math>\mu\in\mathcal{P}(Y)</math>.
* Let <math>\pi : Y\to X</math> be a Borel-[[measurable function]]. Here one should think of <math>\pi</math> as a function to "disintegrate" <math>Y</math>, in the sense of partitioning <math>Y</math> into <math>\{ \pi^{-1}(x)\ |\ x \in X\}</math>. For example, for the motivating example above, one can define <math>\pi((a,b)) = a</math>, <math>(a,b) \in [0,1]\times [0,1]</math>, which gives that <math>\pi^{-1}(a) = a \times [0,1]</math>, a slice we want to capture.
* Let <math>\nu \in\mathcal{P}(X)</math> be the [[pushforward measure]] <math>\nu = \pi_{*}(\mu) = \mu \circ \pi^{-1}</math>. This measure provides the distribution of <math>x</math> (which corresponds to the events <math>\pi^{-1}(x)</math>).

The conclusion of the theorem: There exists a <math>\nu</math>-[[almost everywhere]] uniquely determined family of probability measures <math>\{\mu_x\}_{x\in X} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(Y)</math>, which provides a "disintegration" of <math>\mu</math> into {{nowrap|<math>\{\mu_x\}_{x \in X}</math>,}} such that:
* the function <math>x \mapsto \mu_{x}</math> is Borel measurable, in the sense that <math>x \mapsto \mu_{x} (B)</math> is a Borel-measurable function for each Borel-measurable set <math>B\subseteq Y</math>;
* <math>\mu_x</math> "lives on" the [[fiber (mathematics)|fiber]] <math>\pi^{-1}(x)</math>: for <math>\nu</math>-[[almost all]] <math>x\in X</math>, <math display=block>\mu_{x} \left( Y \setminus \pi^{-1} (x) \right) = 0,</math> and so <math>\mu_x(E) =\mu_x(E\cap\pi^{-1}(x))</math>;
* for every Borel-measurable function <math>f : Y \to [0,\infty]</math>, <math display="block">\int_{Y} f(y) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (y) = \int_{X} \int_{\pi^{-1} (x)} f(y) \, \mathrm{d} \mu_x (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (x).</math> In particular, for any event <math>E\subseteq Y</math>, taking <math>f</math> to be the [[indicator function]] of <math>E</math>,<ref name=Dellacherie_Meyer>{{cite book |author1=Dellacherie, C. |author2=Meyer, P.-A. |title=[[Probabilities and Potential]] |series=North-Holland Mathematics Studies |publisher=North-Holland |location=Amsterdam |year=1978 |isbn=0-7204-0701-X }}</ref> <math display="block">\mu (E) = \int_X \mu_x (E) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (x),</math>which shows that the family <math>\{\mu_x\}_{x \in X}</math> is a [[regular conditional probability]].

==Applications==

===Product spaces===
{{More citations needed section|date=May 2022}}
The original example was a special case of the problem of product spaces, to which the disintegration theorem applies.

When <math>Y</math> is written as a [[Cartesian product]] <math>Y = X_1\times X_2</math> and <math>\pi_i : Y\to X_i</math> is the natural [[projection (mathematics)|projection]], then each fibre <math>\pi_1^{-1}(x_1)</math> can be [[canonical form|canonically]] identified with <math>X_2</math> and there exists a Borel family of probability measures <math>\{ \mu_{x_{1}} \}_{x_{1} \in X_{1}}</math> in <math>\mathcal{P}(X_2)</math> (which is <math>(\pi_1)_*(\mu)</math>-almost everywhere uniquely determined) such that
<math display=block>\mu = \int_{X_{1}} \mu_{x_{1}} \, \mu \left(\pi_1^{-1}(\mathrm d x_1) \right)= \int_{X_{1}} \mu_{x_{1}} \, \mathrm{d} (\pi_{1})_{*} (\mu) (x_{1}),</math>
which is in particular{{Clarify|date=May 2022|reason=Notation "\mu(d x_2[pipe]x_1)" has not been defined}}
<math display=block>\int_{X_1\times X_2} f(x_1,x_2)\, \mu(\mathrm d x_1,\mathrm d x_2) = \int_{X_1}\left( \int_{X_2} f(x_1,x_2) \mu(\mathrm d x_2\mid x_1) \right) \mu\left( \pi_1^{-1}(\mathrm{d} x_{1})\right)</math>
and
<math display=block>\mu(A \times B) = \int_A \mu\left(B\mid x_1\right) \, \mu\left( \pi_1^{-1}(\mathrm{d} x_{1})\right).</math>

The relation to [[conditional expectation]] is given by the identities
<math display=block>\operatorname E(f\mid \pi_1)(x_1)= \int_{X_2} f(x_1,x_2) \mu(\mathrm d x_2\mid x_1),</math>
<math display=block>\mu(A\times B\mid \pi_1)(x_1)= 1_A(x_1) \cdot \mu(B\mid x_1).</math>

===Vector calculus===
The disintegration theorem can also be seen as justifying the use of a "restricted" measure in [[vector calculus]]. For instance, in [[Stokes' theorem]] as applied to a [[vector field]] flowing through a [[compact space|compact]] [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] {{nowrap|<math>\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3</math>}}, it is implicit that the "correct" measure on <math>\Sigma</math> is the disintegration of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure <math>\lambda^3</math> on <math>\Sigma</math>, and that the disintegration of this measure on ∂Σ is the same as the disintegration of <math>\lambda^3</math> on <math>\partial\Sigma</math>.<ref name=Ambrosio_Gigli_Savare>{{cite book |author1=Ambrosio, L. |author2=Gigli, N. |author3=Savaré, G. |title=Gradient Flows in Metric Spaces and in the Space of Probability Measures |publisher=ETH Zürich, Birkhäuser Verlag, Basel |year=2005 |isbn=978-3-7643-2428-5 }}</ref>

===Conditional distributions===
The disintegration theorem can be applied to give a rigorous treatment of conditional probability distributions in statistics, while avoiding purely abstract formulations of conditional probability.<ref name=Chang_Pollard>{{cite journal |last=Chang |first=J.T. |author2=Pollard, D. |title=Conditioning as disintegration |journal=Statistica Neerlandica |year=1997 |volume=51 |issue=3 |url=http://www.stat.yale.edu/~jtc5/papers/ConditioningAsDisintegration.pdf |doi=10.1111/1467-9574.00056 |page=287 |s2cid=16749932 }}</ref> The theorem is related to the [[Borel–Kolmogorov paradox]], for example.
